metadata.name: Ocean Shore Railroad
metadata.note: The Ocean Shore Railway (incorporated 18 May 1905; reorganised as the Ocean Shore Railroad on 9 October 1911 after its 1909 bankruptcy and 1911 sale to bondholders) set out to build a double-track electric railway from San Francisco to Santa Cruz along the San Mateo coast. The 1906 earthquake threw much of the new grade into the sea and the line was never joined: it ran as two disconnected steam railroads - the Northern Division from 12th and Mission Streets, San Francisco, to Tobin (1907) and on to Tunitas Glen (1908), and the Southern Division from Santa Cruz to Scott Creek (1906) and Swanton (1908) - with a Stanley Steamer auto stage over the 26-mile Tunitas-Swanton gap (not drawn). Only the franchise section on San Francisco streets was electrified (600 V DC, worked by electric locomotives); everywhere else, including Santa Cruz, was steam and later gasoline motor cars. All passenger service ended with an employees' walkout on 16 August 1920; abandonment was approved in October 1920.
metadata.mode_note: Northern Division = commuter_rail: a steam railroad (electric locomotives only for the city street section) carrying San Francisco suburban, real-estate and excursion traffic with several trains a day and theatre trains; it was not an electric car line between communities, so not interurban despite its electric-railway charter and Wikipedia's "interurban railways" category. Southern Division = intercity_rail: a rural steam branch with one or two trains a day, later mixed with log traffic.
metadata.ownership_note: One company and one colour (#1695A3, pre-reserved for this railroad). The 1911 change from Ocean Shore Railway to Ocean Shore Railroad was a sale at foreclosure to the same bondholders, who kept running the same trains with the same staff and equipment; it is recorded as a segment boundary, not a Rule 4 split. The Scott Creek Railway (1908) was a paper subsidiary worked with Ocean Shore equipment and is not a separate company here. The Municipal Railway's 1917 emergency steam trains over the Army Street-Daly City part of the line lasted weeks and are recorded as context only.
metadata.geometry_quality: Northern Division 38.6 mi traced vs 38.0 mi documented; Southern Division 15.7 mi traced vs 15.5 mi documented. Real period geometry: OpenHistoricalMap way 200014102 (from the 1915 USGS San Mateo sheet) for Palmetto Avenue to Montara, 15.7 mi; OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=Ocean Shore Railway/Railroad or otherwise railway=abandoned for Montara-Tunitas and Scott-Swanton. Proxies (labelled per feature): San Francisco streets including Alemany Boulevard, which is the railroad's own paved-over right of way (7.0 mi, of which 0.14 mi straight line and 0.75 mi Bayshore Boulevard stand-in); Half Moon Bay Coastal Trail and Highway 1 (5.8 mi); the parallel SP Santa Cruz Branch from Natural Bridges to Davenport (9.1 mi). The Devil's Slide section is drawn on its pre-1916 alignment for all years. All lines checked for reversals, revisits and single-vertex spikes (none).
not_yet_sourced: Running times and timetables for any year - no Ocean Shore public timetable was found online; all avg_speed_kmh values and every headway except 1906 (south) and 1912 (north) are estimates.
Exact Southern Division frequency 1908-1920 and whether passengers were carried only on mixed trains.
Opening date of Scott-Swanton: Brandt (1954) implies May 1906, Whaley (santacruztrains.com) June-July 1908. 1908 used.
Start date of the Tunitas-Swanton auto stage: 1908 (Brandt) vs 1914 (Whaley).
Formal abandonment of the south end: 24 Oct 1920 (Brandt) vs 23 Oct 1920 (Whaley).
The line from Army and Potrero to the shops (via San Bruno/Holladay Avenues) and the post-1916 Devil's Slide relocation are not mapped; both are drawn approximately.
Jim Fergusson's branchline.uk California station list (cited by the Wikipedia route map) returned 403 Forbidden, so station-by-station timetable years were not checked.

metadata.excluded: Not drawn: the Tunitas-Swanton auto stage; freight-only switching of the Potrero district trackage by Muni, SP and WP after August 1920 and the Western Pacific-operated remnant used into the 1980s; the San Vicente Lumber Company's private operation of the south end 1920-1923 and its Little Creek logging line; the unbuilt Golden Gate Park branch and the unbuilt Tunitas-Pigeon Point grade.

properties.line: Ocean Shore: Northern Division (San Francisco – Tobin)
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. No Ocean Shore public timetable with running times was found (Brandt 1954 gives train counts, not times). 30 km/h (about 19 mph) allows for the electric-locomotive street running on 12th Street, Florida Street and Potrero Avenue, an engine change at the shops, and steam running on a curving cliffside line.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 18.5 mi against a documented 18.1 mi (Wikipedia route-map template mileposts: 12th & Mission 0.0, Sixteenth Street 0.8, Twenty-Fourth Street 1.9, Shops 2.5, Onondaga 5.4, Palmetto 7.1, Daly City 7.6, Mussel Rock 11.9, Salada 14.3, Rockaway 16.6, Pedro Valley/Tobin 18.1). Intermediate checks against those mileposts fall within 0.25 mi: Daly City 7.7, Mussel Rock 12.1, Salada 14.1, Rockaway 16.7. SAN FRANCISCO, 7.0 mi, APPROXIMATED ON TODAY'S STREETS: 12th & Mission to Army & Potrero (2.2 mi) is routed on the franchise streets Brandt names - 12th Street, Florida Street, Mariposa Street, Potrero Avenue - over the OSM road graph (0.17 mi of the start runs on 11th/Harrison/Bryant connectors because 12th Street no longer meets Division directly); a 0.14 mi STRAIGHT LINE bridges Potrero Avenue to Bayshore Boulevard across the US-101 interchange; Bayshore Boulevard (0.75 mi) STANDS IN for the line's real route from Army Street past San Bruno and Holladay Avenues to the shops, which does not survive and is not mapped; Alemany Boulevard (3.8 mi, OSM road geometry) is the Ocean Shore's own right of way, which the city bought and paved (Brandt 1954), so it is a good proxy for the alignment from the shops to Palmetto Avenue. PALMETTO AVENUE TO TOBIN, 11.7 mi: OpenHistoricalMap way 200014102 (CC0), digitised from the USGS San Mateo 1915 topographic sheet - real period geometry through Daly City, Thornton, Mussel Rock, Salada, Rockaway and the Pedro Valley cut. OHM dates were not used.

segments.note: The first passenger train ran from 12th and Mission Streets to Tobin (later Pedro Valley) on 2 October 1907 - two coaches behind engine 2, 125 passengers. The company had meant to wait for a through line to Santa Cruz but opened early for revenue after the 1906 earthquake and the 1907 panic. Within San Francisco the franchise required electric haulage: the line from 12th and Mission out 12th Street, Florida Street and Potrero Avenue to the shops near the later Alemany/Bayshore junction (about MP 2.5) was wired at 600 V DC and trains were worked there by electric locomotives 51-53 (51 in service March 1907); steam took over at the shops for the rest of the line. Weekend crowds were so heavy that benches were fitted to flat cars. The Ocean Shore Railway went bankrupt in late 1909 (receiver Fred Stratton) and was sold to its bondholders on 17 January 1911, reincorporating as the Ocean Shore Railroad on 9 October 1911; trains ran throughout. Saturday-night theatre trains were added on 26 October 1910. Headway is an ESTIMATE (no timetable found for these years; Brandt says trains ran "not always on schedule").
sources: Segment-level: Brandt, "Ocean Shore: Reaches the Beaches", The Western Railroader 15:7 (1954), pp. 4-10 - 12th & Mission terminal, franchise and electric-haulage requirement, 600 V DC, motor 51, 2 Oct 1907 first train to Tobin, bankruptcy, 1911 sale, theatre trains.

segments.note: By March 1912 general manager Lee Landis had established a daily service of four trains each way, running on time for the first time, and the line showed a profit of $18,700 for 1912. From 1915 the Municipal Railway's H Potrero streetcars ran over Ocean Shore track on Potrero Avenue (Muni laid a parallel track from 18th to 25th Streets). In the United Railroads strike of August-October 1917 Ocean Shore trains carried Union Iron Works shipyard specials, and from 18 September 1917 the Municipal Railway itself ran 42 daily steam trains with leased Ocean Shore equipment from Army and Potrero to Daly City - a short Muni operation recorded here as context, not drawn as a separate company. Earnings fell nearly 50 percent in 1917 under jitney competition; two gasoline motor cars went into service on the north end in November 1918. The company applied to abandon the north end on 12 August 1920; four days later (16 August) all operating employees walked out and no Ocean Shore train ran again. Abandonment was approved 10 October 1920. Afterwards Muni, then SP and WP, switched the Potrero industrial trackage for freight only - not drawn (Rule 1). Headway 240 is Brandt's 1912 four-trains-each-way figure carried forward; the 1917-1920 frequency is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: Brandt 1954, pp. 12-18 - four daily trains each way (March 1912), H line over Potrero Avenue (1915), 1917 Muni emergency service, gas motor cars Nov 1918, 16 Aug 1920 walkout, 10 Oct 1920 abandonment. The walkout is corroborated by the San Francisco Examiner, 17 Aug 1920, p. 11 ("Ocean Shore Trains Quit Indefinitely"), cited by Wikipedia; that article itself was not read.

properties.line: Ocean Shore: Northern Division (Tobin – Tunitas Glen)
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE; see osrr-north-sf-tobin. No running times found.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 20.1 mi against a documented 19.9 mi (Pedro Valley MP 18.1 to Tunitas MP 38.0, Wikipedia route-map template). Checks: Montara 22.9 (MP 22.8), Princeton 26.2 (MP 26.0), Half Moon Bay 30.2 (MP 30.2). Tobin to Montara (4.1 mi) is OpenHistoricalMap way 200014102, digitised from the USGS San Mateo 1915 sheet - i.e. the ORIGINAL pre-1916 alignment round San Pedro Point and Devil's Slide. LATER-ERA CAVEAT: after the January 1916 slide nearly a mile at Devil's Slide was relocated (Brandt), and the 1916-1920 segment is drawn on the 1915 alignment because the relocation is not mapped. Montara to Tunitas Glen (16.0 mi) is routed by Dijkstra over OSM: 5.6 mi on ways tagged old_railway_operator=Ocean Shore Railway (Cabrillo Highway through Montara-Moss Beach and El Granada, the Coastal Trail grade at Miramar and Half Moon Bay), 4.6 mi on untagged railway=abandoned ways (mostly one 3.0 mi way from Purisima to Lobitos and the pieces from Lobitos to Tunitas), and 5.8 mi of PROXY: 2.8 mi on the Half Moon Bay Coastal Trail, 2.1 mi on Highway 1 (chiefly Moss Beach to Princeton past the airport, where the grade is not mapped) and 0.8 mi on service roads and tracks - these run beside, not on, the railroad. The line ends at the south end of the last mapped grade near Tunitas Creek; the exact Tunitas Glen terminal site is not mapped.

segments.note: Extended south from Tobin in 1908 through the Devil's Slide cliffs and the Pedro Point tunnel: the rails reached Granada (El Granada, the railroad's own planned town) on 23 June 1908, Half Moon Bay in mid-October and Tunitas Glen by the end of 1908 - the farthest south the Northern Division ever got. A 26-mile gap remained to the Southern Division; grading went on toward Pigeon Point but no track was laid. Through passengers rode a Stanley Steamer auto stage between Tunitas Glen and Swanton (Brandt places it from the 1908 opening, santacruztrains.com from 1914 - a SOURCE CONFLICT, recorded not resolved). The stage leg is NOT drawn. Because the 1908 openings were staggered, Granada-Tunitas carried no trains for part of 1908. Headway is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: Brandt 1954, p. 8 - Granada 23 June 1908, Half Moon Bay mid-October 1908, Tunitas Glen by end of 1908, Stanley Steamer shuttle to Swanton. Whaley (santacruztrains.com) - Tunitas Glen late 1908 as the maximum extent; autobus from 1914.

segments.note: Four trains each way daily from March 1912 (Brandt). Large picnic and excursion traffic - the San Francisco mail carriers' picnic of 9 June 1912 to Princeton used nearly every engine on the line. A combined landslide and washout on 15 January 1916 stopped all trains south of Pedro Valley. Headway from Brandt's 1912 figure.
sources: Segment-level: Brandt 1954, pp. 12-14 - four trains daily (1912), 9 June 1912 picnic traffic, 15 Jan 1916 washout.

segments.note: Service south of Pedro Valley resumed to Tunitas on 4 March 1916 after nearly a mile of roadbed at Devil's Slide was relocated at a cost of $300,000 (the geometry here still shows the pre-relocation 1915 alignment - see geometry_quality). Gasoline motor cars from November 1918. Service ended with the employees' walkout of 16 August 1920; abandonment of the north end was approved 10 October 1920. Artichoke growers offered to have SP lease the line; SP declined. Headway is an ESTIMATE carried forward from 1912.
sources: Segment-level: Brandt 1954, pp. 14-18 - 4 Mar 1916 resumption and Devil's Slide relocation, motor cars, 16 Aug 1920 walkout, 10 Oct 1920 abandonment.

properties.line: Ocean Shore: Southern Division (Santa Cruz – Scott)
properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. No running times found; 25 km/h reflects a lightly built steam line with many trestles and, after 1908, mixed trains carrying logs.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 13.5 mi against a documented 12.8 mi to Scott (MP 12.8) / 13.4 mi to Scott Junction (Wikipedia route-map template: Garfield Avenue 0.9, Wilders 3.5, Davenport 10.8). The line is drawn to the south junction of Swanton Road and Highway 1, the Swanton Berry Farm vicinity that santacruztrains.com gives for Scott, so it is best read against the 13.4 mi Scott Junction figure. Santa Cruz streets (1.8 mi): from the West Cliff Drive/Bay Street depot site out Delaware Avenue on OSM road geometry - the line ran out Delaware Avenue (Brandt), but in its own right of way, not necessarily on the street centreline. Natural Bridges to Davenport (9.1 mi) is a PROXY drawn on the surviving Southern Pacific Santa Cruz Branch (OSM railway=rail): the Ocean Shore paralleled the SP Coast Line from just east of Wilder Ranch to Davenport, "on the ocean side throughout" (santacruztrains.com), typically a few hundred feet away - its own grade is not mapped. Two OSM points pin it: the Liddell Creek and San Vicente Creek culvert-tunnels (old_railway_operator=Ocean Shore Railroad, themselves tagged location-approximate), spliced in (0.14 mi). Davenport to Scott (1.9 mi) is Highway 1 on ways tagged abandoned:railway=rail - Highway 1 follows the Ocean Shore grade here (santacruztrains.com). 0.4 mi of path and 0.2 mi of trunk road connectors.

segments.note: Track was laid from Santa Cruz to Davenport between late October 1905 and early 1906, passing under Bay Street and out Delaware Avenue, and on toward Scott Creek during 1906. A special on 18 May 1906 carried 105 University of California civil-engineering students to their summer camp near Swanton; regular service began 15 June 1906 with two trains daily each way. The Santa Cruz terminal was a temporary shelter on West Cliff Drive above the SP yard and later a small depot beside Bay Street; the grand viaduct into downtown was never built. This division was steam-operated throughout - Brandt states the San Francisco street section was the only part of the Ocean Shore ever electrified. (The company paid two instalments toward buying the Santa Cruz Union Traction streetcars in February 1906 but defaulted after the earthquake; it never ran them.) The SP-owned Coast Line Railway, completed to Davenport in 1907, took the cement-plant traffic. Headway 480 is two trains each way in about 16 hours (Brandt, June 1906).
sources: Segment-level: Brandt 1954, pp. 4-6 - Delaware Avenue route, 18 May 1906 special, regular service 15 June 1906 with two daily trains each way, only the SF section electrified, Union Traction instalments. Whaley (santacruztrains.com) - track laying Oct 1905-Jan 1906, Scott Creek reached late 1906, West Cliff shelter and Bay Street depot.

segments.note: Ocean Shore Railroad era (bondholders' company from 1911). Passenger business here "came to a crawl" after 1908 (santacruztrains.com) but was kept up to the end; the photographic record shows mixed trains of logs and passengers. Tickets for the Swanton-Tunitas auto stage were sold at the Bay Street depot. The company applied to abandon the south end on 27 July 1920; the 16 August 1920 walkout ended all Ocean Shore service, and abandonment was approved 24 October 1920 (Brandt; santacruztrains.com says 23 October - a one-day conflict, recorded). Three days later the San Vicente Lumber Company bought the whole south-end trackage and ran it privately as a logging line for about three years - freight only, NOT drawn (Rule 1). Headway 720 is an ESTIMATE (roughly one mixed train each way); no timetable found.
sources: Segment-level: Brandt 1954, pp. 17-19 - 27 Jul 1920 application, 16 Aug 1920 walkout, 24 Oct 1920 approval, sale to San Vicente Lumber Co.; p. 21 photo caption "Mixed train of logs and passengers on southern division". Whaley (santacruztrains.com) - passenger service declining but maintained to the end; formal abandonment 23 Oct 1920.

properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE. Short creek-side extension worked by mixed and log trains; no running times found.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced 2.24 mi against a documented 2.1-2.7 mi (Wikipedia route-map template: Scott 12.8 / Scott Junction 13.4 to Swanton 15.5; santacruztrains.com: "two miles up the creek"). Entirely on OSM abandoned-railway geometry up Scott Creek: 0.4 mi on a way named "Ocean Shore Railway", 0.7 mi of Swanton Road built on the grade, and 1.1 mi of untagged railway=abandoned ways. Ends at the Little Creek confluence (Swanton); the San Vicente Lumber Co. logging line continuing up Little Creek is not drawn.

segments.note: Built in 1908 for the San Vicente Lumber Company's Rancho San Vicente timber: the Ocean Shore amended its articles on 19 June 1908 to add an extension from just beyond Scott to Swanton at the foot of Little Creek, and the last spike was driven on 9 July 1908. The Ocean Shore's Scott Creek Railway subsidiary held part of it during a right-of-way dispute; it was worked with Ocean Shore equipment throughout. Ocean Shore trains ran to Swanton until the end: santacruztrains.com records the last run on 16 August 1920. Swanton was also the southern end of the Stanley Steamer auto stage to Tunitas Glen (not drawn). SOURCE CONFLICT: Brandt (1954) says tracklaying was "completed from Santa Cruz to Swanton" by May 1906 and the 18 May 1906 special ran to the summer school "near Swanton"; Whaley's later and more detailed account dates the Scott-Swanton track to June-July 1908. This feature follows Whaley; the 1906 special may have stopped at Scott Creek. Headway is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: Whaley, "Railroads: Scott Creek Railway" (santacruztrains.com) - 19 Jun 1908 amendment, 9 Jul 1908 last spike; santacruztrains.com Swanton page (via search snippet; page now 404) - last run 16 Aug 1920. Conflicting 1906 date in Brandt 1954, p. 5.
